body: 1989 letter section, Buffett's condensed list of his own errors. (1) Buying control of Berkshire's textile mill because 'the price looked cheap'. The 'cigar butt' approach works only for liquidators: 'never is there just one cockroach in the kitchen' and 'Time is the friend of the wonderful business, the enemy of the mediocre.' (2) Hochschild Kohn department store, bought below book with real-estate and LIFO 'extras' - 'three years later I was lucky to sell the business for about what I had paid.' Lesson: 'It's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price. Charlie understood this early; I was a slow learner.' (3) 'Good jockeys will do well on good horses, but not on broken-down nags'; 'when a management with a reputation for brilliance tackles a business with a reputation for bad economics, it is the reputation of the business that remains intact' (first said in 1980s letters, repeated 1985 with the leaking-boat line: 'energy devoted to changing vessels is likely to be more productive than energy devoted to patching leaks'). (4) 'Easy does it': 'we concentrated on identifying one-foot hurdles that we could step over'; 'we've done better by avoiding dragons than by slaying them.' Exception: 'a marvelous business encounters a one-time huge, but solvable, problem' (AmEx, GEICO). (5) Errors of omission: passing on big purchases he understood - 'the cost of this thumb-sucking has been huge.' Related 1979 line: 'turnarounds seldom turn'. Actionable: a cheap price on a structurally poor Indian business (commodity textiles, sub-scale PSU, leveraged infra) is not a margin of safety; time compounds against you.

data.exception: great business with a one-time solvable problem
key_quotes: Time is the friend of the wonderful business, the enemy of the mediocre.
It's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price.

title: Buffett 1989: 'Mistakes of the First Twenty-five Years' - cigar butts, bad horses, avoid dragons
